newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Afghan Taleban report seizing key airbase, town.
newsitem.headline: Afghan Taleban report seizing key airbase, town.

text.p: Afghanistan's Taleban militia captured a key airbase and a town north of the capital Kabul in a big offensive on Thursday, Taleban sources and witnesses said.

The Taleban sources said their fighters had seized Bagram airbase and the town of Charikar, about 50 km (30 miles) from the Afghan capital, in heavy fighting against forces loyal to ousted president Burhanuddin Rabbani.

But a spokesman for the ousted government's top military commander Ahmad Shah Masood, quoted by Iranian television, denied the fall of Bagram or any change of frontlines there. In Kabul, a Taleban interim government minister said the Islamic movement's leader Mullah Mohammad Omar had made donations to the poor of the capital and three other cities to celebrate Thursday's victory.

Acting Information and Culture Minister Amir Khan Mutaqi told reporters that 100 million afghanis ($3,635) had been made available for Kabul and 50 million afghanis each for Jalalabad, Kandahar and Herat.
A spokesman at Taleban headquarters in the southern city of Kandahar said its forces had captured 500 opposition fighters as they thrust north.
"We are now advancing north of Charikar," Sayed Mohammed Haqqani told the Pakistan-based Afghan Islamic Press (AIP).

Iranian television quoted the spokesman for Masood as rejecting the report about the fall of Bagram and saying there had been no changes in the frontlines between the Taleban and the opposition Supreme Council for the Defence of Afghanistan.
He said the council forces still controlled Bagram.
But witnesses who visited the Taleban's new front line in Charikar, capital of Parwan province, said the town was deserted and there were few signs of fighting.
The area was totally deserted without evidence of much resistance by Masood's forces ...," said a witness who did not want to be identified.
He said he saw bodies of two opposition fighters on the roadside, their mouths stuffed with afghani banknotes -- an act the Taleban does to depict their foes as mercenaries.

Thursday's battle followed three days of inconclusive U.N.-sponsored peace talks in the Pakistani capital of Islamabad between the Taleban, which controls about two-thirds of Afghanistan, and its opponents based in the north.
Wounded fighters on the Taleban side of the frontline said both sides had suffered heavy casualties in the fighting.
"Bagram airbase was captured late this morning and Charikar city has also come under our control," said one.
The Soviet-built airbase and Charikar had been held by the forces of Masood and his powerful ally, northern Uzbek chief General Abdul Rashid Dostum.
Jets from both sides bombed each other's ground positions, Taleban sources said on Thursday.
The fighting was the most intense on the front lines north of Kabul for about three weeks.
AIP reported earlier that at least 12 opposition fighters and three Taleban militiamen had been killed in the battle for Bagram, scene of the heaviest clashes.
It said seven Taleban fighters had been wounded in the two-pronged assault from the Qarabagh area to the south and the village of Bagram to the west of the battered airfield.
Bagram fell to the purist Taleban after they captured Kabul on September 27, but was retaken by Masood on October 18. The Taleban grabbed it back on December 27, but held it for a few hours only.
When opposition forces captured the base in October there were eight apparently useless fighter jets, several transport aircraft and helicopter carcasses on the tarmac.
The base, on a dusty plain with snow-capped peaks in the background, was used by Soviet forces in the 1980s to support a communist-backed government in Kabul.
